## Introduction

Last-mile delivery — the final leg of a shipment from a distribution facility
to the end consumer — is the most expensive and operationally complex segment
of any urban supply chain. In a city like New York, where traffic density,
limited loading zones, and building access constraints compound the challenge,
the proximity of warehouse infrastructure to residential population is a
critical determinant of delivery cost and service reliability.

This analysis asks a straightforward question: **which NYC neighborhoods lack
adequate warehouse coverage, and how many people live in those gaps?**

To answer it, I combine 2020 Census population data at the census tract level
with NYC's own property tax lot database (PLUTO) to map industrial and
warehouse facilities across the five boroughs. I then apply a 1-mile service
radius — a conservative threshold chosen to reflect realistic urban delivery
reach given NYC traffic and parking constraints — and identify tracts that
fall entirely outside that coverage zone.

The 1-mile threshold is intentionally conservative. A 5-mile radius, standard
in suburban logistics models, eliminates virtually all gaps in NYC due to the
city's industrial density. The tighter radius surfaces meaningful variation
and reflects the operational reality that a warehouse 4 miles away in
Manhattan traffic may be effectively unreachable for same-day delivery.

> **Data note (updated October 7, 2026):** An earlier version of this report
> (published October 4) showed 38 gap tracts and 169,223 residents, with 14
> Manhattan gap tracts. Those numbers were wrong. The Socrata API returns
> results in pages, and the initial pull hit the default 1,000-row limit,
> returning an incomplete warehouse dataset. A corrected pull (no row limit)
> retrieved the full PLUTO industrial lot set. With complete data, Manhattan
> has near-complete industrial coverage (only 1 gap tract), and the city-wide
> gap falls to 31 tracts and 61,426 residents. All numbers in this version
> reflect the corrected pull.

---

## Data Sources

All data is pulled programmatically via public APIs. No manual file downloads
are required to reproduce this analysis.

| Dataset | Source | Year | Access Method |
|---|---|---|---|
| Census tract boundaries + population | U.S. Census Bureau (Decennial Census) | 2020 | `tidycensus` R package |
| Borough boundaries | U.S. Census Bureau (TIGER/Line) | 2024 | `tigris` R package |
| Industrial/warehouse tax lots | NYC Dept. of City Planning — PLUTO | Current | NYC Open Data Socrata API |
| Median household income by tract | U.S. Census Bureau (ACS 5-year) | 2020 | `tidycensus` R package |

**A note on the warehouse data:** PLUTO classifies every NYC tax lot by land
use code. This analysis filters for code `06` (Industrial & Manufacturing),
which includes warehouses, distribution centers, and freight terminals. This
is a broader category than warehouses alone — some lots may be light
manufacturing or workshops. It represents the best publicly available proxy
for logistics infrastructure without purchasing commercial real estate data.

---

## Methodology

The analysis follows four steps:

**1. Data acquisition.** Census tract population and geometry are pulled from
the 2020 Decennial Census via the `tidycensus` package. Borough boundaries
come from the Census TIGER/Line files via `tigris`. Industrial lot locations
are queried from the NYC PLUTO dataset via the Socrata JSON API with no row
limit, then converted to point geometry using the lot centroid coordinates.
Median household income is pulled from the 2020 ACS 5-year estimates.

**2. Coordinate reference system.** All layers are projected to EPSG:2263
(New York State Plane, Long Island), which uses feet as its unit of
measurement. This CRS is optimized for accuracy in the New York metro area
and is the standard used by NYC government GIS data.

**3. Buffer analysis.** Each industrial lot centroid is buffered by 5,280
feet (1 mile). The resulting circles are dissolved into a single merged
coverage polygon using `st_union()`. This merged polygon represents the
total area of NYC within 1 mile of at least one industrial facility.

**4. Gap identification.** Each census tract is tested for intersection with
the coverage polygon using `st_intersects()`. Tracts with no intersection
are classified as "far from industrial land." In addition, the straight-line
distance from each tract centroid to its nearest industrial lot is computed
using `st_distance()`, enabling continuous distance-band analysis beyond the
binary classification.

---

## Results

```{r}
#| label: load-results
#| message: false

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(tidyr)

nyc_tracts       <- readRDS(here("data/processed/nyc_tracts_analyzed.rds"))
borough_summary  <- readRDS(here("data/processed/borough_summary.rds"))
warehouses       <- readRDS(here("data/processed/warehouses.rds"))
warehouse_buffer <- readRDS(here("data/processed/warehouse_buffer.rds"))
```

### City-Wide Summary

```{r}
#| label: citywide-summary

total_tracts       <- nrow(nyc_tracts)
underserved_tracts <- sum(!nyc_tracts$served)
underserved_pop    <- sum(nyc_tracts$population[!nyc_tracts$served], na.rm = TRUE)
total_pop          <- sum(nyc_tracts$population, na.rm = TRUE)
pct_underserved    <- underserved_pop / total_pop

cat(
  "Total census tracts:             ", comma(total_tracts), "\n",
  "Tracts far from industrial land: ", comma(underserved_tracts), "\n",
  "Population in those tracts:      ", comma(underserved_pop), "\n",
  "Share of total population:       ", percent(pct_underserved, accuracy = 0.1), "\n"
)
```

Across NYC's 2,327 census tracts, **`r comma(underserved_tracts)` tracts
containing `r comma(underserved_pop)` residents** fall outside a 1-mile
radius of any industrial or warehouse facility. That represents
`r percent(pct_underserved, accuracy = 0.1)` of the city's total population.

### Distance-Band Analysis

The binary gap classification (served vs. not) masks variation in how far
residents actually are from industrial land. This section reports the share
of population within each distance band, by borough, and the median straight-line
distance from tract centroid to the nearest industrial lot.

Two distance measures are in use here and they give different numbers
intentionally. The borough table (below) classifies a tract as "served" if
any part of it intersects a 1-mile buffer -- the most generous possible
reading. The distance table here uses the tract centroid, which is stricter:
a large tract whose center sits 1.1 miles away counts as a gap by centroid
even if its edge is technically within range. The 0.7% city-wide figure
comes from the buffer method; the centroid method shows about 6% of Queens
residents and 12% of Staten Island residents more than a mile from industrial
land.

```{r}
#| label: distance-bands

# Requires dist_to_nearest_miles column added by 02_spatial_analysis.R
bands <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 3)

tracts_with_borough <- nyc_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    borough = case_when(
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "061" ~ "Manhattan",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "047" ~ "Brooklyn",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "081" ~ "Queens",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "005" ~ "Bronx",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "085" ~ "Staten Island",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(population), !is.na(dist_to_nearest_miles), !is.na(borough))

borough_bands <- tracts_with_borough |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(
    within_0.5mi   = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 0.5]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_1mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 1.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_2mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 2.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_3mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 3.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    median_dist_mi = round(median(dist_to_nearest_miles, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_dist_mi))

# City-wide row
citywide_band <- tracts_with_borough |>
  summarise(
    borough        = "NYC (all)",
    within_0.5mi   = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 0.5]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_1mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 1.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_2mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 2.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    within_3mi     = percent(sum(population[dist_to_nearest_miles <= 3.0]) / sum(population), accuracy = 0.1),
    median_dist_mi = round(median(dist_to_nearest_miles, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )

band_table <- bind_rows(borough_bands, citywide_band)

kable(
  band_table |>
    select(
      Borough                    = borough,
      `Within 0.5mi`             = within_0.5mi,
      `Within 1mi`               = within_1mi,
      `Within 2mi`               = within_2mi,
      `Within 3mi`               = within_3mi,
      `Median tract dist. (mi)`  = median_dist_mi
    ),
  caption = "Population share within each distance band, by borough (straight-line distance from tract centroid to nearest industrial lot)"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: distance-chart
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of tract-level distances to nearest industrial lot, by borough"
#| fig-height: 5

nyc_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    borough = case_when(
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "061" ~ "Manhattan",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "047" ~ "Brooklyn",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "081" ~ "Queens",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "005" ~ "Bronx",
      substr(GEOID, 3, 5) == "085" ~ "Staten Island",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(dist_to_nearest_miles), !is.na(borough)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dist_to_nearest_miles, fill = borough)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.8, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~borough, nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 5), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "mi")) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = "Distance to Nearest Industrial Lot, by Borough",
    subtitle = "Straight-line distance from census tract centroid; tracts weighted equally",
    x        = "Distance to nearest industrial lot (miles)",
    y        = "Number of tracts",
    caption  = "Source: NYC PLUTO via Socrata API | U.S. Census Bureau (2020)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text         = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

### Borough Breakdown

```{r}
#| label: borough-table

borough_table <- borough_summary |>
  select(borough, coverage, tracts, population) |>
  filter(!is.na(borough)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = coverage,
    values_from = c(tracts, population),
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `% in Gap` = scales::percent(
      population_Underserved / (population_Served + population_Underserved),
      accuracy = 0.1
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(population_Underserved / (population_Served + population_Underserved))) |>
  select(
    Borough          = borough,
    `Gap Tracts`     = tracts_Underserved,
    `Served Tracts`  = tracts_Served,
    `Pop. in Gap`    = population_Underserved,
    `% in Gap`
  )

kable(
  borough_table,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption     = "Last-mile logistics coverage by borough (1-mile service radius)"
)
```

### Map 1: Population Density

The population density map establishes the baseline: where are people
concentrated across the five boroughs? Manhattan's core shows the highest
densities, exceeding 150,000 persons per square mile in some tracts. The
outer boroughs show more moderate densities with significant variation
between neighborhoods.

```{r}
#| label: map1
#| fig-cap: "NYC population density by census tract, 2020 Decennial Census"

knitr::include_graphics(here("output/maps/map1_population_density.png"))
```

### Map 2: Last-Mile Logistics Gap Analysis

The gap map overlays three layers of information: census tract coverage
status (green = within 1 mile of industrial land, red = outside 1 mile),
the merged 1-mile service radius (light blue halo), and individual
industrial lot locations (blue points).

```{r}
#| label: map2
#| fig-cap: "NYC last-mile logistics gaps — census tracts outside a 1-mile warehouse service radius"

knitr::include_graphics(here("output/maps/map2_logistics_gaps.png"))
```

### Borough-Level Bar Chart

```{r}
#| label: bar-chart
#| fig-cap: "Population outside 1-mile industrial radius, by borough"
#| fig-height: 5

underserved_by_borough <- borough_summary |>
  filter(coverage == "Underserved", !is.na(borough)) |>
  arrange(desc(population))

ggplot(underserved_by_borough,
       aes(x = reorder(borough, population), y = population)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#d6604d", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(population)),
    hjust  = -0.1,
    size   = 3.5,
    color  = "gray30"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Population Outside 1-Mile Industrial Radius, by Borough",
    subtitle = "Residents living more than 1 mile from any industrial/warehouse facility",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Population",
    caption  = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau (2020) | NYC PLUTO via Socrata API"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title         = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

### Income Analysis: Does Wealth Drive the Pattern?

The gap tracts are concentrated in outer Queens and Brooklyn — neighborhoods
like Bayside, Douglaston, and Marine Park. That raises an obvious question:
are these wealthier areas driving warehouses out, or is something else going
on? To test this, I pull 2020 ACS median household income by tract and
compare the income distributions of gap tracts versus served tracts.

```{r}
#| label: income-pull

# Load pre-pulled income data (pulled in 01_data_pull.R)
# Avoids calling the Census API at render time.
income_data <- readRDS(here("data/processed/nyc_income.rds"))

nyc_tracts_income <- nyc_tracts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  left_join(income_data, by = "GEOID") |>
  filter(!is.na(median_income))
```

```{r}
#| label: income-summary

income_summary <- nyc_tracts_income |>
  group_by(served) |>
  summarise(
    tracts        = n(),
    median_income = median(median_income, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(served, "Within 1 mile of industrial land", "Outside 1 mile (gap)"))

kable(
  income_summary |> select(group, tracts, median_income),
  col.names   = c("Group", "Tracts", "Median Household Income"),
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  caption     = "Median household income: gap tracts vs. served tracts (2020 ACS 5-year)"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: income-chart
#| fig-cap: "Median household income distribution: gap tracts vs. served tracts"
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(nyc_tracts_income, aes(x = median_income, fill = served)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#d6604d", "TRUE" = "#7fbf7b"),
    labels = c("FALSE" = "Outside 1 mile (gap)", "TRUE" = "Within 1 mile")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(scale = 1/1000, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(
    title    = "Income Distribution: Gap Tracts vs. Served Tracts",
    subtitle = "2020 ACS 5-year median household income",
    x        = "Median Household Income",
    y        = "Density",
    fill     = "Coverage Status",
    caption  = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2020 5-year estimates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
```

```{r}
#| label: income-interpretation

all_gap_median <- median(
  nyc_tracts_income$median_income[!nyc_tracts_income$served], na.rm = TRUE
)
served_median <- median(
  nyc_tracts_income$median_income[nyc_tracts_income$served], na.rm = TRUE
)

cat(
  "Median income, gap tracts (all NYC):  $", comma(round(all_gap_median)), "\n",
  "Median income, served tracts:         $", comma(round(served_median)), "\n",
  "Gap tracts with income data:          ",
  sum(!nyc_tracts_income$served), "of", sum(!nyc_tracts$served), "\n"
)
```

Gap tracts skew higher-income than served tracts ($`r comma(round(all_gap_median))` vs.
$`r comma(round(served_median))` median household income). That result holds but needs
context: only `r sum(!nyc_tracts_income$served)` of the `r sum(!nyc_tracts$served)` gap
tracts matched to income data, and Queens — not Manhattan — accounts for most of the
gap population (32,622 residents across 13 tracts). Queens gap tracts include outer
neighborhoods like Bayside and Douglaston that are solidly middle-to-upper-middle
income and genuinely distant from industrial land.

The wealth signal is real but the mechanism is geographic, not political. These are
low-density residential neighborhoods at the city's edge, far from industrial corridors,
not wealthy enclaves that pushed industry out. **The gap follows the outer edges of the
city's industrial footprint**, and those edges happen to overlap with more affluent
outer-borough neighborhoods.

---

## Discussion

### Key Findings

Queens accounts for the largest share of population in the coverage gap (32,622
residents across 13 tracts), followed by Brooklyn (19,809 across 11 tracts). The gap
tracts in both boroughs sit at the city's outer edges — neighborhoods like Bayside,
Douglaston, and Marine Park that are far from the industrial corridors concentrated
along the waterfront and freight routes closer to the urban core.

Manhattan has only one gap tract (GEOID 36061000100, Census Tract 1 -- the
Battery Park/financial district waterfront), and it contains zero counted residents.
Census Tract 1 is a dense commercial area, not a park or uninhabited land, so
the zero count is almost certainly a differential privacy artifact from the 2020
Census rather than a true zero population. The borough's near-complete coverage
reflects the density of industrial lots in specific corridors (West Side railyards,
Meatpacking District, Hudson Yards area).

The income data shows gap tracts skew higher-income on average, but this reflects
Queens outer neighborhoods, not Manhattan. The Manhattan gap tract itself has no
usable population count in this dataset.

The distance-band analysis adds resolution to the binary picture: even among
"served" tracts, a meaningful share of the population sits close to the 1-mile
boundary. The distance distribution varies significantly by borough, with Staten
Island and outer Queens showing longer median distances than Manhattan or the Bronx.

### Limitations

**Land use proxy.** PLUTO code `06` captures industrial lots broadly. A more
precise analysis would use actual warehouse operating data from a commercial
source (CoStar, CBRE) or cross-reference with business license data. Real
last-mile operations in Manhattan often run from garages, retail backrooms,
and microhubs classified as commercial or parking in PLUTO — meaning the
true coverage may be better than this analysis shows.

**Edge effect.** This analysis counts only NYC-classified lots. Major
distribution hubs across the Hudson in New Jersey (roughly 1 mile from west
Manhattan) and just outside the city line in Nassau and Westchester are
excluded. This inflates apparent gaps in western Manhattan, Staten Island,
and eastern Queens. The effect is largest for Staten Island: the borough
sits adjacent to major NJ logistics corridors in Elizabeth and Linden, and
its distance numbers would look materially different if cross-Hudson lots
were included.

**The 1-mile cliff.** A tract 1.1 miles from a lot is counted as a gap; one
at 0.9 miles is not. The distance-band table above partially addresses this
by reporting continuous bands, but the binary classification in the maps and
borough table still uses the 1-mile threshold.

**Proximity is not service.** Being within 1 mile of an industrial lot does
not mean being well-served. Delivery reach depends on street network
connectivity, curb access, building entry, and operating hours — none of
which are in this dataset. Straight-line distance is not travel time.

**No cost or feasibility.** Identifying a gap area does not mean a
micro-fulfillment center belongs there. Rent levels, zoning restrictions,
and curb access make many gap areas economically impractical regardless of
demand.

### Supply Chain Implications

As a first-pass screen of where NYC's industrial land is relative to its
population, this analysis is useful. As a recommendation for where to site
logistics infrastructure, it needs the additional context above.

The practical next step is converting straight-line distances to road-network
travel times, which would replace the proximity proxy with a measure closer
to actual service reach. A retailer or 3PL evaluating NYC market entry needs
that layer — along with demand data and real operating constraints — before
the gap locations in this analysis become actionable.

---

## Reproducibility

All data is pulled from public APIs at runtime. To reproduce this analysis
from scratch:

```r
# 1. Install packages and create folder structure
source("setup.R")

# 2. Pull all data from APIs
source("analysis/01_data_pull.R")

# 3. Run spatial analysis (computes served/unserved and dist_to_nearest_miles)
source("analysis/02_spatial_analysis.R")

# 4. Export maps
source("analysis/03_maps.R")

# 5. Render this report
quarto::quarto_render("report/index.qmd")
```

**R version:** `r R.version$version.string`
**Key packages:** tidycensus `r packageVersion("tidycensus")`,
sf `r packageVersion("sf")`,
ggplot2 `r packageVersion("ggplot2")`
